extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys/agents, and applicants preparing patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for drafting independent, dependent, multiple-dependent, and related claim types to define scope, satisfy clarity and patentability requirements, and manage prosecution/amendment strategies across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying breadth of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying the breadth of claims can offer insurance against arguments that a patent is invalid based on the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting claims of differing scope (broad independent claims plus narrower dependent claims) helps defend against prior art discovered later (e.g., during infringement litigation) that might destroy the broad claim but not the narrower ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim should specify essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim should typically specify the essential features needed to define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although standards vary by office, features implied by generic terms may not need explicit recitation (e.g., a bicycle claim need not mention wheels). Where patentability depends on a technical effect, include all technical features essential for that effect. Claims must be clear and directed to the heart of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims must necessarily lead to the claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a process for producing a product X, the process claimed should be such that, when carried out reasonably by a person skilled in the art, it necessarily leads to product X as its end result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed process does not inevitably produce the claimed product, there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims for well-known kinds may identify product and modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a product claim, if the product is of a well-known kind and the invention lies in modifying it, it is typically sufficient that the claim clearly identifies the well-known product and specifies what is modified and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar considerations apply to apparatus claims; clearly identify the known product and the modifications that embody the inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft a combination of broad independent and narrower dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters commonly prepare a combination of broad and narrow claims by first drafting the broadest independent claim and then drafting dependent claims covering various narrower scopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims act as a practical fallback if prior art defeats a broad independent claim; narrower dependent claims may still allow the applicant to obtain useful protection and commercial advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim format signals dependency and reduces repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim is one that 'depends from' another claim and refers to a parent claim (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising...'), which includes everything from the parent claim plus whatever is newly recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This format makes the dependent claim more concise by avoiding repetition of the whole parent claim. Dependent claims tend to be considerably shorter than independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims are always narrower than the claim from which they depend
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims can only add elements or limitations to the claim from which they depend; they cannot subtract or broaden the parent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of improper dependent claim: a dependent claim that states 'wherein the light is not attached to the pencil' would subtract an essential element and is therefore improper. Dependent claims must not extend the scope of protection of the corresponding independent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three permitted ways for a dependent claim to state additional features
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately after the reference to another claim, a dependent claim states at least one additional feature by: (i) adding at least one new element (typically 'further comprising E'); (ii) selecting at least one element from a broader element in the parent claim (typically 'wherein E is E1') or further characterizing an element; or (iii) a combination of (i) and (ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding a light to a pencil (further comprising); narrowing 'light' to 'LED light' (wherein); or both adding and narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims must refer back to at least one previous claim and cannot refer forward
rubrics_metrics.description: All dependent claims must refer back to at least one previous claim and they cannot refer forward to a subsequent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangement and numbering must ensure clear dependency (claim trees help visualize relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Group and arrange dependent claims to enable ready reckoning and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims should be grouped together in the most appropriate way possible so that their association and meaning can be readily understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The arrangement must enable a ready reckoning and construction of related claims and their meaning; use logical groupings to simplify understanding and later amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims serve as a prosecution fallback and can be converted to independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims reflect the 'fallback' position: if an examiner finds prior art that denies patentability to a broad independent claim but not to a dependent claim, the applicant may obtain a patent by cancelling the rejected independent claim and drafting a new independent claim by combining limitations from the allowable dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are provided showing renumbering and amendment formats (deleted words strikethrough, new words underlined). Amendment procedures vary by jurisdiction; dependent claims may be renumbered and amended to become independent when client approves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims can support a broader interpretation of independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim can be used to support a broader interpretation of an independent claim by clarifying that the independent claim can cover alternatives beyond what the dependent claim specifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Claim 1 recites 'a box' and dependent Claim 2 recites 'wherein the box is wooden'; the dependent clarifies but also implies Claim 1 could be wooden or nonwooden. This can help arguments about support/enablement, although an opponent might argue lack of support for alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims with two-part and Markush independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dependent claim depends on an independent claim written in the two-part format (separated by 'characterized in that'), the dependent claim includes everything in both parts and the 'characterized by' phrase is unnecessary (though permissible). For Markush independent claims, a dependent claim may define a narrower subset of the Markush group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include two-part claims for writing devices and Markush group narrowing for chemical claims (selecting specific R groups). Dependent claims narrow the broader set by specifying members of the Markush group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims: format and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A multiple dependent claim refers to more than one claim in the alternative (e.g., 'the apparatus of Claim 1 or Claim 2' or 'of one of Claims 1 and 2'), meaning it depends from either claim but not both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The body of a multiple dependent claim must narrow the claim(s) from which it depends. A multiple dependent claim covers embodiments that satisfy any one of the parent claims to which it refers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible and impermissible phrasing for multiple dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Many expressions are accepted to refer to more than one claim in the alternative (e.g., 'according to Claim 1 or Claim 2', 'as in any of the preceding claims in which...'). Wording that would cause the claims to become cumulative is not permitted (e.g., 'according to Claims 1 and 2', 'according to Claims 1–3', 'as in Claims 1, 2 and/or 3').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cumulative formulations that would improperly broaden or combine claims; use alternative phrasing to limit dependency to alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pros and cons of multiple dependent claims including fee implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple dependent claims usually reduce the countable number of claims, which can affect client decisions because claim fee structures differ by office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the US, multiple dependent claims trigger extra fees and are uncommon; at the EPO they may save fees due to countable claim numbering. Using multiple dependent claims may also facilitate certain amendments (e.g., in the EPO) but excessive use (multiple-multiple dependencies) can complicate comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-multiple dependent claims permissibility varies by jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO, Japan) permit multiple-multiple dependent claims (a multiple dependent claim serving as a basis for another multiple dependent claim), while others (e.g., United States, Republic of Korea) do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when drafting multiple-multiple dependencies; check local rules to ensure permissibility and to avoid drafting claims that will be disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claims may refer to features of another claim in some jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) an independent claim may contain a reference to another claim, thereby incorporating defined features of the other claim without being a dependent claim. In other jurisdictions (e.g., United States), an independent claim cannot contain a reference to any other claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'Apparatus for carrying out the process of Claim 1' or 'Plug for cooperation with the socket of Claim 1'. Verify permissibility in jurisdictions of interest and review whether incorporated features are essential to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional references for multiple claim types (useful for computer-implemented and pharmaceutical inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitional references (e.g., 'a data-processing apparatus comprising means for carrying out the method as defined in Claim 1' or 'a computer program product comprising instructions which... cause the computer to carry out the method as defined in Claim 1') incorporate method claim features into other claim categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is commonly used to draft comprehensive protection across claim types (method, apparatus, computer program product, storage medium) and in pharmaceuticals (compound, composition, method of manufacture, medical use). A single dependent claim can incorporate features of multiple preceding claims by reference to 'any one of Claims 1–4', etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claim patentability can affect examination of related process/use claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO), if a claimed process results in a product defined by a product claim and the product claim is patentable, no separate examination for novelty and inventive step of the process claim is necessary provided the process inevitably results in the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This also applies to uses of products when the product is patentable and used with claimed features. In other instances, patentability of one claim does not imply patentability of the other; check the relevant office practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sets can be reasoned about using set theory and Venn diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims establish boundaries of technical subject matter (peripheral claiming); their relationships (independent vs dependent) can be illustrated by set theory (subsets, overlaps) and Venn diagrams to show scopes and embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use set representations to visualize how dependent claims form subsets of independent claims, how dependency chains and dependency pyramids arise, and how specific embodiments map into claim scopes. This assists drafting and later interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze claim dependency relationships to assess validity and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of dependency relationships among patent claims is helpful to patent examiners assessing validity (novelty, inventive step) and to judges when validity of granted patents is challenged, and it is also helpful when assessing infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim trees, dependency charts and scope diagrams to identify which claims may remain novel in light of prior art and which claims an accused product might infringe; examples illustrate situations where some dependent claims remain novel while independent claims do not.
